findings: A (cone driven to the bottom of the bed at every point) dies on: "how many blows take it to a hundred millimetres"; "The floor is 130 millimetres of washed silica sand"
B (weight dropped by hand from a height chosen per point) dies on: "a steel cone on a rod, under a ring weight raised to a collar and let fall"

D (arena-to-arena spread wider than the spread between his two visits) dies on: "The gap between my February morning and my July afternoon is still wider than the gap between this school and any other school I test."
justification: Key C is stated outright: two-thirds as deep is a shallower first blow and a nearly doubled count is a higher count. A dies on the instrument's stated stopping depth (100 mm) against the stated bed depth (130 mm); B dies on the fixed drop height (raised to a collar); D is the exact reversal of Pallenmoor's quoted comparison. Every non-key option is contradicted by a stated fact, none is merely unmentioned. Key C support: "in the cold the first blow took the cone two-thirds as deep, and the count nearly doubled"

findings: A (wax worn off the grains lower down) dies on: "the wax he brought up from the bottom was in better condition than the wax at the top"
B (sand broken down finer than specification) dies on: "the grains he sieved came out much as the original specification had them"

C (bed below the tines stayed loose, out of reach of hoofprints) dies on: "Eighty millimetres of it had not been turned since the day it was laid, and under nine years of hoofprints it had gone firm enough to lean a spade on."
justification: Key D is the cored-sample result in figures (about 8 per cent top, nearer 3 lower down). A, B and C are each the direct negation of a stated finding: bottom wax in better condition, grains as specified, and the unturned 80 mm gone firm under hoofprints. No second option survives. Key D support: "In the top 50 millimetres the fibre came out at about 8 per cent by weight; lower down it was nearer 3."

findings: A (sprinkler schools are newer, sand has had less wear) dies on: "He has the same pair of grids from a hundred and forty other arenas, some of them older than this one."; "The waxed ones move, whatever their age."

C (a membrane under them holds water in and stops the bed drying) dies on: "laid over a membrane and crushed stone"; "Both figures moved, and they moved together"; "The waxed ones move, whatever their age."; "kept damp with a sprinkler"; "The wax is a paraffin blend, and it is doing most of that work."

D (they are read at other hours so the change falls between the grids) dies on: "He has the same pair of grids from a hundred and forty other arenas"; "the morning grid and the afternoon grid sit almost on top of one another"
justification: REWRITTEN OPTION C VERIFIED REFUTED, NOT MERELY UNMENTIONED. The passage's only membrane is under the school being tested - 'laid over a membrane and crushed stone' - and that school is on the moving side of the contrast ('Both figures moved, and they moved together'; 'The waxed ones move, whatever their age'). So the one arena known to have a membrane is an arena whose two grids separate, which contradicts the option's causal claim that a membrane is what keeps a bed steady through the day; the inference runs backwards from the moving side to the stable side. The passage also states the actual damp mechanism - the schools are 'kept damp with a sprinkler', a continuous external input, not water held in from below - and names the operative variable outright ('The wax is a paraffin blend, and it is doing most of that work'). C therefore cannot become a second defensible answer: to be defensible it would need a membrane attached to the sprinkler schools and to stability, and the text attaches its only membrane to a mover. Key B is supported by the two-sided contrast (plain sand and fibre kept damp = grids on top of one another; waxed = move) with the causal agent named, and the same sentence that kills A ('whatever their age') also isolates wax as the variable, so the key's support is at least as strong as the strongest distractor refutation (A, age explicitly ruled out). D dies on 'the same pair of grids' - the comparison schools are read on the same two clocks. Key B support: "In the schools laid on plain sand and fibre and kept damp with a sprinkler, the morning grid and the afternoon grid sit almost on top of one another."; "The waxed ones move, whatever their age."; "The wax is a paraffin blend, and it is doing most of that work."

findings: B (reads the yard's later actions as an answer to the soundness question) dies on: "The yard has changed one thing and left the other alone."; "he says he would argue it from the veterinary literature rather than from his own figures"; "The tester measures a surface; there is no horse above the cone."

C (treats the riders' account as what the readings were brought in to correct) dies on: "Then there is the machine, though not in the way the yard had blamed it."; "The yard has blamed the machine, then the mix, then the man on the tractor."; "Below about six degrees the coating is stiff, the grains lock together, and a hoof breaks the surface."
D (rates the brochures the fuller answer to the yard's question) dies on: "That is a good deal less than the trade’s brochures offer, and it is worth more than they are."
justification: Key A is the writer's own superlative: the care - the limits he sets on his figures - is the most useful thing about him. B is refuted by her own characterisation of what the yard did ('changed one thing and left the other alone') and by the text's statement that the soundness claim is argued from the veterinary literature, not the readings. C is refuted by what the readings actually corrected: the yard's blaming, not the riders, whose January-hard / July-deep report the wax mechanism confirms. D is the softest of the three - the clause concedes the brochures offer more - but the writer's rating is the second half of the same sentence ('it is worth more than they are'), so D is contradicted, not merely unsupported. Key A support: "Here Pallenmoor is careful, and the care is the most useful thing about him."

findings: A (grains probably freezing to one another in the cold) dies on: "Below about six degrees the coating is stiff, the grains lock together, and a hoof breaks the surface."; "He read a grid of thirty points at seven, with the school at three degrees"; "The wax is a paraffin blend, and it is doing most of that work."

B (a heated school will ride in February much as in July) dies on: "Above about twenty-five it goes slack, the grains slide past one another, and the floor gets deep."; "deep and tiring by a July afternoon"; "Heaters have been costed and not ordered: the quote came to more than a month of winter lessons."; "I can’t put a number on it; these readings won’t carry one"
D (the tractor may matter more than the temperature) dies on: "The temperature is doing more in that room than the tractor is,"
justification: Key C names the two drivers the text establishes: temperature (both penetrometer figures move with it, and the wax thresholds explain how) and tine depth (tines at 50 mm in a 130 mm bed sorted the bed into a loose layer on a hard one). A dies on the stated mechanism - the wax coating stiffening, at a cold reading of three degrees, above freezing - not water freezing. B dies on the two-ended wax curve: the July deep state needs the slack end above twenty-five, which a winter heater ('a month of winter lessons') does not deliver, and the text refuses the extrapolation outright. D is the verbatim reversal of Pallenmoor's quote. Key C support: "The leveller’s tines were set to 50 millimetres."; "Harrowing lifts fibre, and fibre keeps sand from packing, so the machine had been slowly sorting the bed into a loose layer riding on a hard one."; "Both figures moved, and they moved together"

findings: A (Hence - makes the ending a consequence of the start) dies on: "and again there has been no signal"
B (Rather - corrective, displacing the preceding clause) dies on: "the ending is unanimous"; "and again there has been no signal"
D (Elsewhere - locative, another place) dies on: "five seconds later the sound stops"
justification: The frame fixes the discourse relation mechanically: 'again' marks a second instance of the same signal-free unanimity, which is what 'Equally' encodes. 'Hence' would make the unanimous ending a consequence of the unanimous start, but the sentence presents it as a repetition; 'Rather' needs something to correct and both clauses stand; 'Elsewhere' needs another place and the second clause is five seconds later in the same hall. Key C support: "and again there has been no signal"

findings: B (cut (in) - to interrupt) dies on: "for the length of one clap you are alone with an opinion nobody asked for"
C (fall (in) - take a place in a formation) dies on: "No one has agreed to anything, there is no conductor to watch"
D (break (in) - to intrude) dies on: "for the length of one clap you are alone with an opinion nobody asked for"
justification: The risk named in the clause is isolation - being left alone mid-clap - so the missing action is participation: 'join in'. 'Cut in' and 'break in' both mean interrupting, the wrong direction entirely for a room that fails to respond. 'Fall in' presupposes an order or formation to take a place in, which the passage explicitly denies (nothing agreed, no conductor); bare 'fall in' is not the joining idiom. Key A support: "That is why the second pair of hands matters more than the first: it turns a private view into a public event."

findings: A (transaction - an exchange of value) dies on: "about how long is decent, conducted at speed and without words"
C (bargain - the outcome reached, and takes 'over', not 'about') dies on: "about how long is decent, conducted at speed and without words"; "the sound comes down faster than it went up"
D (settlement - the result, not the process) dies on: "about how long is decent, conducted at speed and without words"; "the sound comes down faster than it went up"
justification: The slot is the coming-down itself - a wordless process 'conducted at speed' and, decisively, 'about how long is decent'. A negotiation is about something; a settlement is of something, a bargain over something, and a transaction is an exchange with no norm as its subject. Bargain and settlement are result nouns where the frame needs the process, which the preceding clause describes as it happens. Key B support: "Nobody wants to be the last pair of hands still going, so the sound comes down faster than it went up"

findings: A (rehearsed) dies on: "No one has agreed to anything, there is no conductor to watch"; "A hall organises itself in about a fifth of a second, and not one of the people in it could explain how."
B (outspoken) dies on: "conducted at speed and without words"
C (brief) dies on: "it is not permitted to run long"; "Four or five seconds, then a ragged tail"
justification: 'Although X, it is not permitted to run long' needs X to pull against the limit, and the passage supplies the warmth a child performer gets - audibly not the sound a stranger gets. 'Brief' is co-directional with 'not permitted to run long', so the concession collapses; 'rehearsed' is denied by the unagreed, conductorless, unexplainable half-second; 'outspoken' requires speech from a phenomenon the text defines as wordless. Key D support: "and everybody present can hear that it is not the same sound the recorder player got"

findings: A (narrowly - by a small margin) dies on: "A room asked for a big hand for a stranger will give one"; "and everybody present can hear that it is not the same sound the recorder player got"

C (instinctively - unprompted) dies on: "A room asked for a big hand for a stranger"; "The clapping in the school hall starts a beat before the recorder has stopped, and it starts everywhere at once."
D (eagerly - with enthusiasm) dies on: "and everybody present can hear that it is not the same sound the recorder player got"
justification: The room complies with a request and the result is audibly lesser: 'dutifully'. 'Eagerly' is the direct opposite of the audible deficit named in the same sentence. 'Instinctively' is excluded by 'asked for' and by the contrast with the genuinely unprompted opening clap. 'Narrowly' has no margin to attach to in the frame - the room does give the hand, and the shortfall the clause names is in kind, not degree. Key B support: "A room asked for a big hand for a stranger will give one"; "and everybody present can hear that it is not the same sound the recorder player got"

findings: B (a spoilt sample can be seen on the ward by its colour) dies on: "Nothing shows on the ward; the colour comes with the spinning."
C (blood gases go by tube because they cannot wait) dies on: "Blood gases have never gone by tube; a porter walks those down."
D (rejects fell once the loop was slowed) dies on: "The loop runs at the speed it always has."; "Two bins are lined with foam, and rejects are down by about half."
justification: Key A is Ashvenor's own attribution, with the accelerometer week behind it. B, C and D are each flatly negated by a sentence of the passage: nothing shows on the ward, blood gases have never gone by tube, and the loop runs at the speed it always has with the fall in rejects attributed to foam-lined bins. Key A support: "It’s the stop at the far end that does it"; "Between stations the shocks were tiny."

findings: A (the neighbour answered without bringing the railway plan in) dies on: "The neighbour’s attorney enclosed a tracing of the railway company’s deposited plan."
B (the quarrel began because the thorn was left untended) dies on: "cut from above by one and cleaned from below by the other"; "both sides agree the thorn was last laid in 1839"

C (the surveyor came after the attorneys began writing) dies on: "The previous October a surveyor had chained and pegged the line along the bank, from the ash to the culvert."; "In November 1845 Ephraim Ruddiforth’s attorney claimed the bank, the ditch and the timber from the stone gap down to the lane."
justification: Key D is carried by the landmark identity the passage plants (ash in the stone gap, culvert at the lane): the claim runs stone gap to lane, the pegged line ash to culvert - the same stretch. A is negated by the enclosed tracing; B by the stated joint maintenance and the agreed 1839 laying, which was common ground rather than a grievance; C by the explicit chronology, the survey being 'the previous October' to a November 1845 claim. Key D support: "An ash grew in the stone gap; a culvert ran under the lane."; "In November 1845 Ephraim Ruddiforth’s attorney claimed the bank, the ditch and the timber from the stone gap down to the lane."; "The previous October a surveyor had chained and pegged the line along the bank, from the ash to the culvert."

findings: B (ensemblens invandning ar ett svepskal) dies on: "Ett svepskäl är det inte."
C (utoka antalet textade kvallar i ensemblens takt) dies on: "Fler särskilda kvällar begär jag inte."; "Att ensemblen vänjer sig vid remsan kan jag inte lova."
D (skarm aven ovanfor lilla scenen) dies on: "Om lilla scenen kan bära samma sak vet jag inte."; "och något förslag för den scenen har jag inte"
justification: Key A is the article's stated proposal plus its stated concession: text on every performance on the big stage, while granting that the strip locks the line and that the cost is real. B is negated word for word ('Ett svepskäl är det inte'); C by the refusal to ask for more special evenings and by the explicit refusal to promise the ensemble will get used to it; D by the writer saying she does not know whether the small stage can carry it and has no proposal for it. Key A support: "Från och med nästa spelår bör texten gå på varje föreställning på stora scenen, inte på fyra utvalda."; "Textremsan låser repliken."; "Ändå ska den bäras."

findings: A (raden ar markt med slingans symbol) dies on: "Slingans symbol finns längst ned på varje uppslag i programbladet och har gjort det i alla år."

B (raden upprepas langst ned pa varje uppslag) dies on: "Slingans symbol finns längst ned på varje uppslag i programbladet och har gjort det i alla år."; "har de textade föreställningarna en egen rad, inklämd mellan syntolkning och skolföreställningar"
C (raden anger vem som skoter tekniken) dies on: "Längre bak i programbladet står Ingegerd Hörnfeldt under rubriken Text och teknik."
justification: Key D restates the opening sentence. The three distractors are attribute swaps, each landing on something the passage places elsewhere: what sits at the foot of every spread is the loop symbol, not the row (killing both A and B, since the row is a single line in the autumn programme); and the technician is named further back under her own heading, not on the row. Key D support: "har de textade föreställningarna en egen rad, inklämd mellan syntolkning och skolföreställningar"

findings.killing_span: En hov samlar hela djurets tyngd på en yta stor som en tallrik, och mot det hjälper varken broddar eller lättare lass.
findings.category: refuted: span explicitly negates the option
findings.note: Broddar are named and their help is denied by 'varken ... eller'. The option's exact remedy is the one the text rules out.

findings.killing_span: Lassen gick på kälke i stället, och kälken drogs för hand.
findings.note: The text assigns the same 'i stället' slot the option claims, but to hand-drawing, not to horses; reinforced by 'Hästen fick stå i stallet.'

findings.option_text: Hästarna användes till annat under de veckorna.
findings.note: Scope-aligned: the stable sentence covers exactly the skare period the option scopes itself to ('under de veckorna'). Standing in the stable is incompatible with being put to other use. The passage additionally contains no other horse-activity sentence (only mention of 'häst' in the text), so nothing re-opens it.

justification: Key A ('Hovarna sjönk igenom där folk gick.') is carried near-verbatim by 'Skaren som bar en karl gick sönder under hoven', with 'ett djur som trampade igenom skar upp benen på iskanten' confirming the sinking-through and 'En hov samlar hela djurets tyngd på en yta stor som en tallrik' supplying the mechanism. All three non-key options die on cited spans: B on an explicit negation, C and D on incompatible assertions. No second option is defensible. Cross-question check: neither rewritten q2 option revives any of B/C/D - q2 C ('på skidor') would, if wrongly accepted, cut against C rather than support it, and the only lexical bridge from q2 D ('körningen', which can connote horse-hauling in rural Swedish) cannot revive C or D because the passage explicitly assigns the hauling to a hand-drawn kälke and the horse to the stable. Every span above was verified as a byte-identical, uniquely-occurring substring of the passage before writing.

findings.option_text: Hushållen turades om och delade på slitet.
findings.killing_span: Var gård körde för sig, och sällan väntade någon in grannen.
findings.note: Per-farm working and not waiting for the neighbour is incompatible with taking turns and sharing the load.

findings.option_text: Lassen släpades fram på skidor över myren.
findings.killing_span: Skidor dög till att ta sig fram med, men inte till att dra med.
findings.category: refuted: span explicitly negates the option
findings.note: REWRITE CHECKED. The passage now states both halves of the ski function - good for travelling on ('ta sig fram med'), explicitly not for dragging with ('men inte till att dra med') - so the option's operative claim is explicitly negated, not merely unaddressed. The only occurrence of 'Skidor' in the passage is this negating sentence. The named ground is genuine but inert: 'Myren bär' and 'löper morgonens väg som två upphöjda ryggar tvärs över myren' establish that loads did cross the myr, while 'det som kälkmedarna packat håller emot' and 'Lassen gick på kälke i stället, och kälken drogs för hand.' identify the runners as a hand-drawn kälke. The true locative therefore supports the crossing without supporting the claim about what dragged the loads.

findings.option_text: Inte förrän sista lasset var hemma tog körningen slut.
findings.killing_span: Ett lass som inte är hemma vid tio blir liggande till nästa natt.
findings.note: REWRITE CHECKED. The deadline is stated as a rule with a consequence: the ten-o'clock cutoff ('Man ger sig i väg vid fyra, i mörker, och vid tio är det över.') plus the named penalty for missing it. The passage thus asserts the exact counter-case the option denies - hauling ends at ten whether or not the last load is home, and a load that is not home is left out until the next night.

justification: Key B ('Det gick inte att bestämma dagarna i förväg.') is carried by a three-span cluster: 'Veckorna kom när de kom.', 'Somliga år blev det fyra morgnar på hela vintern, och ett par vintrar uteblev skaren.' and 'Man såg på himlen och bestämde sig kvällen innan.' - the decision point is stated outright as the evening before, read off the sky. All three non-key options die on cited spans: A and D on incompatible assertions, C on an explicit negation. No second option is defensible. The prior silence defect on C is resolved: the passage no longer merely fails to mention skis dragging loads, it states what skis were and were not good for, and the added locative ('över myren') is separately attested without lending the option its drag claim. Every span above was verified as a byte-identical, uniquely-occurring substring of the passage before writing.
